claims.text: Above 900 °C, protective-scale formation in CrFeCoNiX is controlled by the X element's effects on cation diffusion kinetics and oxide-phase stability at the metal/oxide interface.
The single-phase versus multiphase microstructural state modulates local cation-diffusion paths.
Changes in local cation-diffusion paths caused by microstructure govern oxide-scale continuity and adhesion.
A minor Al addition to a single-phase CrFeCoNi alloy promotes a continuous Al2O3 or mixed Cr2O3-Al2O3 scale.
Al addition reduces the outward mobility of deleterious cations.
Al addition enhances adhesion at the oxide/alloy interface.
Al2O3 is protective, grows more slowly than chromium oxide, and is comparatively stable in aggressive high-temperature environments.
In AlCoCrFeNi, Al and Cr form passivating oxides whose alpha-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 concentrations increase with time before approaching steady state.
Mn has high cation mobility in the relevant CrFeCoNiMn alloys and exposure regime.
Mn addition promotes localized segregation and faster differential diffusion.
A multiphase microstructure promotes localized segregation and differential cation diffusion relative to a single-phase state.
Segregation and uneven diffusion produce discontinuous oxide scales with localized stress accumulation.
The stress-prone scales generated by Mn addition or multiphase microstructures crack or spall during high-temperature exposure.
Single-phase Al-added alloys will form continuous, slowly growing, adherent scales dominated by Al2O3 and possibly Cr2O3.
CrFeCoNi without X is expected to form predominantly chromia with mixed oxides.
The X-free CrFeCoNi baseline scale is less coherent and more prone to spallation than the single-phase Al-added scale.
Above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3.
The proposed comparison applies to CrFeCoNi-based single-phase and multiphase alloys exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
Equivalent exposures at 950–1050 °C can compare Al-, Mn-, and Si-added variants against an X-free baseline using scale morphology, composition, adhesion, and cation profiles.

A lack of improved scale coherence or adhesion in single-phase Al-added samples, together with no detectable diffusion or oxide-stability difference from controls, would refute the proposed mechanism.
